distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer disease leaf for invasive bloodstream infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, independent of the presenting source or later complication label.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: Necrotizing fasciitis, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, cellulitis, pneumonia, postpartum sepsis, endocarditis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, meningitis, and deep abscess are source/context/complication/mimic or separate leaves. They may be represented as axes and event hazards when clinically observed, but they are not appended to this disease name.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking should use ordinary clinical observations available at the tested stage: fever or hypothermia, chills, abrupt toxic appearance, skin/soft tissue or mucosal source signs, oral-maxillofacial inflammation, peripheral ischemic wound context, vital signs, CBC, CRP/PCT, lactate, renal/liver/coagulation injury, and observed complications. Blood culture species, susceptibility, emm typing, and final source adjudication are confirmatory/non-ranking unless a post-workup test explicitly includes them.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Barrier or mucosal invasion by Streptococcus pyogenes
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: GAS crosses skin, soft tissue, pharyngeal, oral, genital tract, surgical, traumatic, or ulcerated barriers and enters lymphatics or blood. The portal can be obvious, subtle, or initially occult.
Density and persistence of viable Streptococcus pyogenes in blood; drives blood culture positivity, abrupt systemic illness, and opportunities for deep or endovascular seeding.

Complement, neutrophil, monocyte, IL-1/TNF/IL-6, and acute-phase activation in response to invasive GAS; produces fever, rigors, tachycardia, CRP/PCT rise, leukocyte changes, and constitutional symptoms.
Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins and related virulence factors can amplify cytokine release, capillary leak, coagulopathy, tissue injury, and shock. Activity varies by strain and host context.

Distributive shock, endothelial leak, hypoperfusion, mitochondrial dysfunction, AKI, ARDS, encephalopathy, hepatic injury, thrombocytopenia, and DIC-like coagulopathy from invasive GAS and host response.

Cellulitis, erysipelas, oral-maxillofacial cellulitis, wound infection, infected ulcer, postpartum endometritis, septic arthritis, myositis, abscess, or necrotizing soft tissue infection can be the source of bacteremia or a concurrent focus.
Persistent bloodstream infection can seed valves, prosthetic material, joints, bone, meninges, deep soft tissue, brain/subdural spaces, or other sterile sites.

Undrained abscess, necrotic tissue, infected ischemic ulcer, retained device, postpartum uterine focus, severe oral disease, or endovascular focus can continue to seed blood despite antimicrobial activity.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Inactive, delayed, or poorly delivered antimicrobial therapy
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Delay before active therapy, lack of toxin-suppressive adjunct when toxin physiology is dominant, allergy constraints, underdosing, poor tissue delivery to ischemic/necrotic foci, or rare non-susceptibility contexts can prolong viable burden.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Barrier invasion is the route into blood.
Local tissue infection can seed bacteremia.
Viable organisms in blood raise culture positivity; species identity remains confirmatory unless post-workup mode is tested.
Higher viable burden and uncontrolled source prolong positive cultures.
Bloodstream burden triggers systemic innate inflammation.
High invasive burden increases systemic toxin exposure when the strain expresses relevant virulence factors.
Pyrogenic cytokines cause fever; older or immunosuppressed hosts may be blunted.
Abrupt bacteremia commonly produces chills or rigors.
Fever, inflammation, hypovolemia, and shock raise heart rate.
Fever, metabolic acidosis, hypoperfusion, or respiratory complications increase respiratory rate.
Cytokines produce toxic appearance, malaise, prostration, and fatigue.
Systemic infection and toxin physiology can produce nausea and vomiting.
Systemic infection, toxin physiology, or antimicrobial exposure can produce diarrhea; it is not required for GAS bacteremia.
Leukocytosis is common, though leukopenia can occur in severe GAS sepsis.
Neutrophilic response tracks invasive bacterial inflammation.
CRP rises in invasive pyogenic infection.
PCT often rises in invasive bacterial sepsis.
Inflammation and capillary leak lower albumin.
Toxin-amplified cytokine release drives shock and organ dysfunction.
High viable invasive burden can drive sepsis physiology even without toxin-dominant features.
Distributive shock and capillary leak lower blood pressure.
GAS sepsis can cause hypotension and vasopressor requirement.
ARDS, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or shock-related respiratory failure can lower oxygen saturation.
Sepsis, hypoperfusion, fever, and metabolic injury can cause confusion or lethargy.
Hypoperfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction raise lactate.
Sepsis-associated AKI raises creatinine.
Hypoperfusion, dehydration, AKI, and catabolic stress raise BUN.
Shock liver, myositis, or systemic injury can raise AST.
Shock liver or systemic injury can raise ALT.
Severe GAS sepsis can cause thrombocytopenia through DIC, endothelial injury, and critical illness.
DIC-like coagulopathy or hepatic injury can prolong INR.
DIC and thrombosis/fibrinolysis raise D-dimer.
Skin or limb cellulitis, erysipelas, wound infection, or ulcer can be visible around presentation.
Oral or maxillofacial source can produce face, eyelid, submandibular, or masticator-space cellulitis.
Periodontal disease or oral mucosal injury can provide a portal for invasive GAS.
Recent or active pharyngitis/URI can precede invasive GAS.
Postpartum endometritis or uterine infection is a recognized source context for invasive GAS.
Ischemic ulcer or necrotic toe context lowers local defense and can seed bacteremia.
Some GAS tissue infections progress to necrotizing infection.
Toxin-amplified cytokine release can cause shock.
Hypotension, capillary leak, and high lactate raise shock hazard.
Hypoperfusion and inflammatory renal injury raise AKI hazard.
Sepsis, pneumonia, capillary leak, or fluid resuscitation can precipitate ARDS.
GAS sepsis may produce DIC-like coagulopathy.
Sepsis-associated coagulopathy can progress to purpura fulminans and ischemic tissue loss.
Persistent bacteremia creates metastatic and endovascular seeding risk.
Bloodstream spread can seed sterile sites.
GAS endocarditis is rare but possible, especially with valve or device substrate.
Uncontrolled nidus prolongs bacteremia.
Necrotic tissue, abscess, dental source, ischemic ulcer, or uterine source may require source control.
Inactive or delayed therapy prolongs viable burden.
When therapy is inactive or delayed, active coverage is low.
Shock and organ dysfunction are major lifespan hazards.
Uncontrolled nidus increases death risk.
Deep metastatic or endovascular complications increase mortality.
Delayed active therapy worsens invasive GAS outcomes.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Severe systemic infection, shock, hypoxemia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, or fluid overload can increase oxygen or ventilatory support needs; this parallels the existing oxygen_saturation pathway.

axes.shape_free_text: Probability that blood cultures are positive for a bacterial bloodstream infection. Organism species and susceptibility remain confirmatory unless testing post-workup evidence.
Duration of persistent GAS-positive blood cultures under the disease context; ordinary species identity remains confirmatory.
Fever or hypothermia in invasive GAS bacteremia.
Chills, rigors, or abrupt shaking fever with bacteremia.
Tachycardia from fever, inflammation, hypovolemia, or shock.
Tachypnea from fever, acidosis, shock, or pulmonary complication.
Systolic blood pressure; may fall with distributive shock.
Diastolic pressure; may fall in vasodilatory shock.
Mean arterial pressure; low values mark shock physiology.
Oxygen saturation; can fall with ARDS, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or shock.

Oxygen or ventilatory support requirement: 0 room air, 1 low-flow nasal cannula, 2 mask or higher low-flow support, 3 high-flow nasal cannula, 4 noninvasive ventilation, 5 invasive ventilation or extracorporeal support.
Confusion, disorientation, lethargy, stupor, or encephalopathy during invasive GAS.
Toxic appearance, weakness, lethargy, malaise, or prostration.
Nausea or vomiting during systemic infection or toxin physiology.
Diarrhea during invasive illness or antimicrobial exposure; not a defining feature of GAS bacteremia.
Observed cellulitis, erysipelas, soft-tissue swelling, wound infection, tender erythema, or infected ulcer of an extremity/trunk/breast/skin site.
Facial, eyelid, cheek, submandibular, masticator-space, or oral-maxillofacial cellulitis/swelling that may serve as source context.
Periodontal disease, oral mucosal scratch, denture trauma, dental extraction need, or other oral portal observed clinically.
Recent or active sore throat, pharyngitis, tonsillitis, otitis, sinusitis, or upper respiratory portal context.
Postpartum fever, abdominal/pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, uterine tenderness/enlargement, endometritis, or necrotic uterine source context.
Ischemic limb, necrotic toe, diabetic/vascular ulcer, cold foot, or poor-perfusion wound that can serve as portal and source-control problem.
Pain localized to infected soft tissue, wound, limb, oral-maxillofacial site, joint, abdomen/pelvis, or deep seeded focus.
WBC count; GAS bacteremia often raises WBC but severe sepsis or immunosuppression can blunt or lower it.
Absolute neutrophil count in invasive bacterial inflammation.
Neutrophil fraction; often elevated with invasive bacterial infection.
Platelet count; thrombocytopenia marks severe GAS sepsis, DIC, TSS-like physiology, or marrow disease context.
Hemoglobin; anemia is not defining but is common with chronic disease, critical illness, bleeding, or host comorbidity.
C-reactive protein in invasive pyogenic infection.
Procalcitonin in invasive bacterial sepsis.
Albumin falls with inflammation, capillary leak, poor nutrition, or chronic disease.
Lactate rises with hypoperfusion and severe sepsis.
Creatinine rises with AKI, shock, CKD, or nephrotoxic context.
BUN rises with dehydration, hypoperfusion, catabolism, CKD, or AKI.
AST can rise with shock liver, myositis, rhabdomyolysis, or systemic injury.
ALT can rise with shock liver or systemic injury.
PT/INR rises with DIC-like coagulopathy, liver dysfunction, anticoagulation, or severe sepsis.
D-dimer rises with DIC, sepsis-associated coagulopathy, thrombosis, or tissue injury.
Hazard of hypotensive shock, vasopressor requirement, or circulatory collapse.
Hazard of AKI from shock, DIC, nephrotoxins, or severe infection.
Hazard of ARDS or severe hypoxic respiratory failure in invasive GAS sepsis.
Hazard of overt DIC or severe sepsis-associated coagulopathy.
Hazard of purpura fulminans, acral ischemia, gangrene, or thrombotic skin necrosis from severe GAS sepsis-associated coagulopathy.
Hazard that local GAS soft tissue infection progresses to necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or myonecrosis. This is a complication/event axis, not the disease name.
Hazard of septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, meningitis, subdural empyema, deep abscess, or other metastatic seeded focus.
Hazard of GAS infective endocarditis; rare but relevant with valve/device substrate or persistent bacteremia.
Probability that current antimicrobial regimen is active against the bloodstream isolate and reaches relevant tissues.
Probability that GAS isolate is susceptible to penicillin or narrow beta-lactam therapy; usually high, but should be evidence-driven if susceptibility is available.
Probability that isolate is susceptible to clindamycin for toxin-suppressive adjunctive use; inducible or constitutive resistance can limit effect.
History of severe immediate beta-lactam reaction or severe delayed reaction constraining beta-lactam therapy.
Need for drainage, debridement, extraction, removal of infected material, hysterectomy/washout, amputation, or other source control.
Adequacy of source control after drainage, debridement, extraction, removal, or surgical management.
Availability and feasibility of IVIG when toxin-mediated shock physiology is dominant.

Lifespan outcome hazard driven by shock, toxin physiology, AKI, ARDS, DIC, necrotizing soft tissue infection, metastatic/endovascular seeding, delayed active therapy, source-control failure, age, and host comorbidity.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and tachycardia co-move through cytokine and sympathetic tone.
Both often track inflammatory burden, but WBC can be blunted or low in severe sepsis.
High D-dimer with thrombocytopenia and prolonged INR raises DIC hazard.
Active therapy shortens bacteremia when source control is adequate.
Adequate source control reduces ongoing bloodstream seeding.
Undrained, necrotic, oral, postpartum, or ischemic sources increase death risk if uncontrolled.
Shock is a major lifespan hazard.
AKI raises treatment complexity and mortality.
DIC raises bleeding, ischemic, and multiorgan failure risks.
Necrotizing infection increases mortality through source-control failure and toxin physiology.
Metastatic seeded foci increase morbidity and mortality.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Beta-lactam effect depends on isolate susceptibility.
Severe beta-lactam reaction may preclude penicillin.
Necrotic or undrained foci may not clear with antimicrobial therapy alone.

failure_modes: poor delivery into necrotic or ischemic tissue

side_effects.interpretation: Allergic reaction context can limit therapy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Pathogen-directed bactericidal therapy when susceptibility and allergy context allow.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Effect requires active coverage and adequate exposure.
Severe beta-lactam reaction may preclude cephalosporin use.

failure_modes: delayed de-escalation decisions due to missing cultures

side_effects.interpretation: Cephalosporins can raise transaminases or cholestatic markers.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad beta-lactam option while bloodstream isolate and source context are being clarified, and a definitive option if susceptible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Toxin-suppressive effect depends on susceptibility and achievable exposure.
Toxin physiology increases value of protein-synthesis inhibition as adjunct.
Adjunctive clindamycin should not replace bactericidal active therapy for bacteremia.

failure_modes: late use after toxin physiology established

side_effects.interpretation: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea and C. difficile risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct to bactericidal therapy when toxin-mediated shock, necrotizing tissue infection, or severe invasive GAS physiology is present or strongly suspected.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Linezolid must be active and should be paired appropriately in severe bacteremia contexts.
Linezolid can be considered when clindamycin resistance or intolerance limits toxin-suppressive adjunct.
Thrombocytopenia increases monitoring burden during linezolid therapy.

failure_modes: use without adequate bactericidal/source-control plan in high-burden disease

side_effects.interpretation: Linezolid-associated thrombocytopenia risk, especially with longer courses.

treatments.context_specific_role: Protein-synthesis-inhibiting option when clindamycin is unavailable, resistant, or not tolerated; not a semantic replacement for source control.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Empiric regimen helps only if it covers the true bloodstream pathogen.
Antibiotics alone may fail in necrotic, oral, abscess, uterine, device, or ischemic sources.

side_effects.interpretation: Renal toxicity risk depends on selected agents and host context.

treatments.context_specific_role: Initial coverage for unstable sepsis before organism, source, and susceptibility context are confirmed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Benefit is largest when an uncontrolled nidus exists.
Incomplete debridement, drainage, extraction, or removal leaves ongoing seeding.

failure_modes: delayed intervention in necrotizing or ischemic tissue

side_effects.interpretation: Procedural bleeding risk depends on coagulopathy and operative extent.

treatments.context_specific_role: Drainage, debridement, oral extraction, uterine source control, device removal, vascular/limb intervention, or other procedure when observed source context requires it.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: IVIG can only influence the vector field when available and delivered.
Toxin-mediated shock context increases possible benefit.

failure_modes: lack of source control or active antibiotics

side_effects.interpretation: Infusion volume and osmotic load may worsen oxygenation in renal/cardiac dysfunction.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunctive antitoxin immune support for severe toxin-mediated shock physiology; should not replace active antimicrobials or source control.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Older age increases invasive infection mortality.
Fever response may be lower in older adults.
Diabetes increases skin/soft tissue and ulcer infection risk.
Diabetes increases AKI vulnerability in sepsis.
Ischemic ulcers provide a portal and source-control problem.
Ischemic tissue may require procedural management or remains a nidus.
Skin break, abrasion, wound, or trauma can be a portal.
Traumatized tissue can be a locus for invasive GAS tissue disease.
Oral mucosal disease can act as a portal for systemic infection.
Oral or sinus source may manifest as maxillofacial cellulitis.
Marrow disease can distort WBC response.
MDS can lower platelet baseline before sepsis.
Early postpartum state is a high-risk mucosal source context for GAS.
Pregnancy-associated invasive GAS can deteriorate rapidly.
Recent GAS throat exposure or pharyngitis can precede invasive disease.
Delay prolongs bacteremia and inflammatory exposure.
Delayed control worsens severe invasive GAS outcomes.

supportive_care: Serial vital signs, mental status, urine output, CBC with differential, platelets, CRP/PCT when available, lactate, creatinine/BUN, electrolytes, AST/ALT, bilirubin, PT/INR, fibrinogen, and D-dimer when severe sepsis or coagulopathy is suspected.
Obtain blood cultures and source cultures before antibiotics when feasible, but do not delay antimicrobial therapy in unstable patients.
Hemodynamic resuscitation with balanced fluids, vasopressors, lactate-guided reassessment, and ICU monitoring when shock physiology is present.

Early source evaluation: skin/soft tissue exam, oral/dental/maxillofacial exam when plausible, postpartum pelvic/uterine assessment, wound/ulcer assessment, imaging for abscess/necrotizing infection, and echocardiography or deep-focus imaging when persistent bacteremia or focal signs occur.
Respiratory support from oxygen through mechanical ventilation for ARDS, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or shock-related respiratory failure.
Renal support and dose adjustment for AKI or CKD; monitor nephrotoxic antimicrobial combinations.
DIC/coagulopathy management with platelet, plasma, fibrinogen/cryoprecipitate, anticoagulation, or surgical timing decisions according to bleeding/thrombosis context.
Infection-control and contact evaluation according to local invasive GAS guidance, especially postpartum, neonatal, household, or institutional clusters.
